title: Νοσῶν καὶ ἰατρός
titleEn: The Sick Man and the Doctor
part: The Sick Man and the Doctor (Chambry 249 · Perry 170)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 249 (= Perry 170). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Νοσῶν τις καὶ ἐπερωτώμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἰατροῦ πῶς διετέθη, ἔλεγε πλέον τοῦ δέοντος ἱδρωκέναι.
sentences.tr: Nosōn tis kai eperōtōmenos hypo tou iatrou pōs dietethē, elege pleon tou deontos hidrōkenai.
sentences.l: A certain man being sick, and being asked by the doctor how he had been faring, said that he had sweated more than was needful.
sentences.i: A man was ill, and when the doctor asked how he had been doing, he said he had sweated more than he should.
sentences.n: διατίθεμαι is 'to be put in such and such a condition', so πῶς διετέθη is simply 'how did he do?'. πλέον τοῦ δέοντος, 'more than the needful', is a standing phrase: the articular participle τὸ δέον stands in the genitive of comparison. ἱδρωκέναι is a perfect infinitive in indirect statement after ἔλεγε.

sentences.l: And he said: « This is good. »
sentences.n: ὁ δέ, the bare article with δέ, is the ordinary Greek for 'and the other one' when the speaker changes — no pronoun is needed. The doctor's three identical verdicts are the fable's engine.

sentences.t: Ἐκ δευτέρου δὲ ἐρωτώμενος πῶς ἔχοι, ἔφη φρίκῃ συνεχόμενος διατετινάχθαι.
sentences.tr: Ek deuterou de erōtōmenos pōs echoi, ephē phrikēi synechomenos diatetinachthai.
sentences.l: And being asked a second time how he was, he said that, being gripped by a shivering-fit, he had been shaken through and through.
sentences.i: Asked a second time how he was, he said a fit of shivering had hold of him and had shaken him to pieces.
sentences.n: ἔχω with an adverb means 'to be in such a state', so πῶς ἔχοι is 'how he was'; the optative is the regular shift in an indirect question after a past main verb. φρίκη is the shuddering of an ague. διατετινάχθαι is the perfect infinitive of διατινάσσω, 'shake violently apart'.

sentences.t: Ὁ δέ· « Καὶ τοῦτο, ἔφη, ἀγαθόν. »
sentences.tr: Ho de· « Kai touto, ephē, agathon. »
sentences.l: And he: « This too, » he said, « is good. »
sentences.n: The verb of saying is left out of the frame and dropped inside the quotation instead — ὁ δέ alone carries 'and the other'. Chambry prints the ἔφη within the guillemets, and it is kept there.

sentences.t: Τὸ δὲ τρίτον ὡς παρεγένετο καὶ ἐπηρώτα αὐτὸν περὶ τῆς νόσου, διαρροίᾳ περιπεπτωκέναι ἔφασκε.
sentences.tr: To de triton hōs paregeneto kai epērōta auton peri tēs nosou, diarroiāi peripeptōkenai ephaske.
sentences.l: And the third time, when he came and was questioning him about the sickness, he kept saying that he had fallen into a flux.
sentences.i: The third time, when the doctor came and asked after his illness, he told him he had come down with a flux of the bowels.
sentences.n: τὸ τρίτον is an adverbial accusative, 'for the third time'. περιπίπτω takes the dative of what one falls in with, almost always something unwelcome. ἔφασκε is the imperfect of φάσκω, the verb of repeated saying — he kept telling him so.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος « ἀγαθὸν καὶ τοῦτο » φήσας ἀπηλλάγη.
sentences.tr: Kakeinos « agathon kai touto » phēsas apēllagē.
sentences.l: And that man, having said « this too is good », took himself off.
sentences.i: And the doctor said, « This too is good, » and went his way.
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖνος is καὶ ἐκεῖνος by crasis. ἀπηλλάγη is an aorist passive used intransitively — 'he got himself away', a common shape in Greek where English has a plain active.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ οἰκείων τινὸς παραγενομένου πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ πυνθανομένου πῶς ἔχοι, ἔφη πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ἐγώ σοι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀπόλωλα. »
sentences.tr: Tōn de oikeiōn tinos paragenomenou pros auton kai pynthanomenou pōs echoi, ephē pros auton· « Egō soi hypo tōn agathōn apolōla. »
sentences.l: And one of his own people having come to him and inquiring how he was, he said to him: « I, I tell you, am undone by the good things. »
sentences.i: And when one of his household came and asked how he was, he said to him: « I tell you, it is the good things that have been the death of me. »
sentences.n: σοι is the ethical dative — a dative that names the person the speaker is appealing to and has no English equivalent but 'I tell you'. ἀπόλωλα is the second perfect of ἀπόλλυμι and is intransitive with present force: 'I am done for'.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπὶ τούτοις ὑπὸ τῶν πέλας μακαρίζονται τῇ ἔξωθεν οἰήσει, ἐφ’ οἷς αὐτοὶ παρ’ ἑαυτοῖς τὰ μάλιστα δυσφοροῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō polloi tōn anthrōpōn epi toutois hypo tōn pelas makarizontai tēi exōthen oiēsei, eph’ hois autoi par’ heautois ta malista dysphorousin.
sentences.l: Thus many among men are called blessed by those near them, on the opinion formed from outside, for those very things over which they themselves, within themselves, are most of all distressed.
sentences.i: Thus many men are counted fortunate by their neighbours, who judge from the outside, for the very things that weigh on them most heavily within.
sentences.n: οἱ πέλας, 'those nearby', is the regular Greek for one's neighbours. ἡ ἔξωθεν οἴησις: the article makes an adjective out of the adverb, 'the notion from outside', so the dative is the ground the neighbours go on. ἐπὶ τούτοις … ἐφ’ οἷς is a correlative pair, the relative picking up what the demonstrative held open. τὰ μάλιστα is adverbial, 'most of all'.
